texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Abstract
texts.text: Abstract

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) has been used in infants with bronchiolitis for decades. Recently, high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy was introduced. We conducted a trial of 50 children with bronchiolitis who were randomized to treatment with CPAP or HFNC. Objectives were to compare the development in respiratory rate, pCO2, and Modified Woods Clinical Asthma Score (M-WCAS) in young children with bronchiolitis, treated with CPAP or HFNC. Secondarily, to compare Neonatal Infant Pain Score (NIPS), treatment duration, treatment failure, and hospitalization length. Median age at inclusion was 2.8 (CPAP group) vs 2.1 months (HFNC group). Mean baseline pCO2 was 6.7 in both groups and mean respiratory rate was 60 vs 56 in the CPAP and HFNC group respectively. No differences were observed in development of respiratory rate, pCO2, or MWCAS.NIPSwashigher in the CPAP group. Treatment failure was scarce in both groups. No significant differences in treatment duration or length of hospitalization were observed.
texts.text: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) has been used in infants with bronchiolitis for decades. Recently, high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy was introduced. We conducted a trial of 50 children with bronchiolitis who were randomized to treatment with CPAP or HFNC. Objectives were to compare the development in respiratory rate, pCO2, and Modified Woods Clinical Asthma Score (M-WCAS) in young children with bronchiolitis, treated with CPAP or HFNC. Secondarily, to compare Neonatal Infant Pain Score (NIPS), treatment duration, treatment failure, and hospitalization length. Median age at inclusion was 2.8 (CPAP group) vs 2.1 months (HFNC group). Mean baseline pCO2 was 6.7 in both groups and mean respiratory rate was 60 vs 56 in the CPAP and HFNC group respectively. No differences were observed in development of respiratory rate, pCO2, or MWCAS.NIPSwashigher in the CPAP group. Treatment failure was scarce in both groups. No significant differences in treatment duration or length of hospitalization were observed.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Conclusion : In infants and young children with bronchiolitis, HFNC may be an effective and pleasant alternative to CPAP. Larger multicenter studies are needed to further explore differences in treatment failure and treatment duration.
texts.text: Conclusion : In infants and young children with bronchiolitis, HFNC may be an effective and pleasant alternative to CPAP. Larger multicenter studies are needed to further explore differences in treatment failure and treatment duration.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Introduction
texts.text: Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Viral bronchiolitis is often caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and is a major cause of disease burden in infants and young children. RSV infections present with symptoms from mild coryza to fulminant respiratory failure and are a major cause of hospitalization in young children. Thus, in Denmark, approximately 3% of children under 2 years of age experience at least one hospitalization due to RSV [4]. Because of airway obstruction, alveolar atelectasis, decreased oxygenation, and increased respiratory work, some children progress to severe respiratory distress and need for noninvasive respiratory support or mechanical ventilation.
texts.text: Viral bronchiolitis is often caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and is a major cause of disease burden in infants and young children. RSV infections present with symptoms from mild coryza to fulminant respiratory failure and are a major cause of hospitalization in young children. Thus, in Denmark, approximately 3% of children under 2 years of age experience at least one hospitalization due to RSV [4]. Because of airway obstruction, alveolar atelectasis, decreased oxygenation, and increased respiratory work, some children progress to severe respiratory distress and need for noninvasive respiratory support or mechanical ventilation.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In Denmark, the standard treatment for infants and young children with respiratory distress due to moderate to severe bronchiolitis has for many years been continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). Although not fully understood, CPAP may work by small airway distension, mucus wash out, and delivery of high flow oxygen [13]. CPAP has been shown to lower respiratory rate and pCO2 better than standard care [14] and has been associated with decreased intubation rates [3]. However, the therapy requires special staff skills, close monitoring, and can be stressful to the child.
texts.text: In Denmark, the standard treatment for infants and young children with respiratory distress due to moderate to severe bronchiolitis has for many years been continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). Although not fully understood, CPAP may work by small airway distension, mucus wash out, and delivery of high flow oxygen [13]. CPAP has been shown to lower respiratory rate and pCO2 better than standard care [14] and has been associated with decreased intubation rates [3]. However, the therapy requires special staff skills, close monitoring, and can be stressful to the child.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Recently, high flow oxygenation therapy (HFNC) was introduced as an alternative tool in the management of respiratory distress due to bronchiolitis. HFNC delivers a heated, humidified gas with a mixture of oxygen and air, washes out dead space, and has some CPAP effect [11]. In a few bronchiolitis studies, HFNC proved to be better than standard care [1] [7]. Furthermore HFNC has been shown to give a better patient tolerance, less nose damage, and less work for the staff than CPAP [12].

HFNC delivers a heated, humidified gas with a mixture of oxygen and air, washes out dead space, and has some CPAP effect [11]. In a few bronchiolitis studies, HFNC proved to be better than standard care [1] [7]. Furthermore HFNC has been shown to give a better patient tolerance, less nose damage, and less work for the staff than CPAP [12].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We conducted a two-center prospective open randomized trial of HFNC and CPAP to explore effects of treatment with these two systems on respiratory variables in infants and young children with bronchiolitis.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Bronchiolitis was defined as an acute respiratory illness in children < 2 years of age presenting with characteristic patterns of wheeze and cough. Criteria for respiratory support were based on clinical and paraclinical signs of respiratory failure: High respiratory rate (RR), retractions, recurrent apnea, hypercapnia, and acidosis.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The study was conducted between December 2015 and May 2018. During the first two seasons, the study took place at the pediatric department at the Hospital of South West Jutland, Denmark, and during the last seasons also at the department of pediatrics at Kolding Hospital, Denmark.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: All children fulfilling the inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria were invited to participate. Because of the nature of this study, blinding was not possible. Randomization was conducted in blocks of four, stratified per center, and treatment allocation envelopes were stored in sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes, prefabricated by a person outside the study. By mistake, the first 20 patients were however randomized by simple lot, conducted by a person outside the study.

texts.orig: Modified Woods Clinical Asthma Score (M-WCAS) [15] is a combined score (0 -10) used to evaluate the degree of respiratory distress in children with bronchiolitis. M-WCAS has been validated for use in hospitalized children with bronchiolitis and includes evaluation of oxygen saturation, inspiratory breath sounds, expiratory wheezing, use of accessory respiratory muscles, and cerebral function [2].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Neonatal Infant Pain Score [5] (NIPS) was used in the last season of inclusion in children younger than 2 months. The score is a validated system based on facial mimic, cry, breathing habitant, arm and leg tonus, and consciousness. A total of 0 -8 points can be achieved, where 0 represents no pain, and eight maximal pain. The children were scored shortly after initiation of therapy and then once daily. For children older than 2 months, the 0 -10 point Face Leg Activity Cry and Consolability (FLACC) score [6] was used.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Sample size calculation was conducted based on the primary outcome pCO2. Assuming a difference of one kPa at 48 h and considering an α error of 5% and a β error at 20%, a sample size of 48 participants was calculated.
texts.text: Sample size calculation was conducted based on the primary outcome pCO2. Assuming a difference of one kPa at 48 h and considering an α error of 5% and a β error at 20%, a sample size of 48 participants was calculated.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For group comparisons, two-sided Student ' s t test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used for normally and nonnormally distributed data respectively. Chi 2 test was used for binary outcomes.
texts.text: For group comparisons, two-sided Student ' s t test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used for normally and nonnormally distributed data respectively. Chi 2 test was used for binary outcomes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Developments in RR, pCO2, M-WCAS, FiO2, and pain scores (NIPS, FLACC, and combined pain score) were measured using a random intercept model with maximum likelihood estimation. Device, time, and interaction between these were chosen as explanatory variables. Post estimation analysis was conducted using residual diagnostics. For the primary outcomes, the model was then extended with season and site, to explore effects of these.

For the primary outcomes, the model was then extended with season and site, to explore effects of these.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: During the study period, a total of 266 children were hospitalized with RSV-related disease. Of these, 99 children were treated with CPAP/HFNC for viral bronchiolitis at the two sites and 50 children were included in the study (22 HFNC/ 28 CPAP). During the first 48 h, ten children left the study. Eight children (5 CPAP/3 HFNC) left due to cessation of need for respiratory support and two children (both CPAP) left because of disease progression leading to transmission to the PICU. Four of the ten children were withdrawn during the first 24 h, including the two children in need of intensive care and one from each group due to cessation of need for respiratory support.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: During the first treatment day, NIPS was lower in the HFNCgroup right after initiation of therapy but declined with time in both groups (Table 2). There was however an overall effect of system in the regression model (coefficient -0.94. p < 0.05) meaning that NIPS was overall lower in the HFNC group. FLACC score was not analyzed, due to the few children assessed with this score. The combined pain score showed similar results as NIPS (Table 2).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In this study, no differences were found in the primary outcomes, suggesting that HFNC may be a good alternative to CPAP in children with bronchiolitis. Our study suggests a better patient acceptance of HFNC compared with CPAP as measured by the NIPS and the combined pain score, which corroborate earlier findings [9, 12]. Sarkar et al. [12] also found less nose damage with HFNC, an outcome not investigated in the present study.

texts.orig: To our knowledge, only few studies compared CPAP and HFNC in management of bronchiolitis. In a retrospective study, Pedersen et al. found that CPAP was superior to HFNC in lowering RR and FiO2 [10]. A multicenter study including 142 children found a higher success rate in the group treated with CPAP [9]. However, two other small studies [8, 12] found the two systems equally effective in lowering of RR, PCO2, etc.

texts.orig: In Denmark, there is a strong tradition for CPAP, and it is likely that it is used in less sick children than elsewhere, which could hamper the comparison between studies. However, CPAP/HFNC was not used more frequently in the years of this study, compared with the two previous seasons [10]. Whether some of the less sick children would have benefited equally to conservative treatment (oxygen, feeding supply, etc.) is a question that goes beyond the purpose for this study.

However, we see no signs of clinically relevant differences in our primary outcomes (Fig. 1). Moreover, the size of our study population is comparable with or bigger than for other studies [8, 12].

texts.orig: Only half of the children admitted with viral bronchiolitis and treated with CPAP/HFNC were included in the study. The major cause was failure to obtain informed consent from both parents because only one of the parents/legal guardians was present at the hospital. texts.orig: The 48-h observation period in our study was chosen to minimize treatment termination within the period, as it was expected that most children would need at least 48 h of treatment. Moreover, we expected that the main effects would occur during this time span. The termination of treatment before 48 h in ten children may have affected the results. However, the dropouts were relatively equally distributed between the two groups, and furthermore, it was only children from the CPAP group who left due to a deterioration of the condition resulting in intensive care. Overall, we do not consider that dropouts during the first 48 h affected the results in favor of HFNC.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Despite a clinically relevant difference of 25 h, no statistically significant difference in treatment length between the groups was found. We suppose that this is primarily due to the lack of power in our study. However, the transferal of two children from the CPAP group to PICU (who therefore were withdrawn from the analysis) may have contributed to the difference in average treatment length. In the present study, treatment failures were few and equally distributed in the two groups. This is in contrast to earlier findings. In a retrospective study, Pedersen et al. [14] found a higher failure rate within the HFNC group, and in a multicenter study including 142 children, Milesi et al. found a higher success rate in the group treated with CPAP [9].

texts.orig: As our study was not powered to show non-inferiority, our results should be followed up, preferably by larger multicenter studies with statistical power to explore this. Also, clinically relevant outcomes like treatment duration, treatment failure, and intubation rates could not be investigated sufficiently in the present study. Hereby, possible differences in patient acceptance, side effects, and staff resource costs within the different treatment systems could be the aim for further investigation.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In conclusion, we found HFNC to be a safe and effective tool for respiratory support in young children with moderatesevere bronchiolitis. We found similar effects on RR, MWCAS, and pC02 compared with CPAP. Pain scores were significantly lower in the HFNC group indicating better patient acceptance. More research is warranted to further explore target groups for each of the two systems.
